steps.say: Let's start with the big idea. A class is a recipe. An object is the cake you bake from that recipe. One recipe, as many cakes as you want.
Every object has three things. A name, so you can find it. Properties, which are its data. And methods, which are the things it can do.
Here is the Stack from your course. Look at __init__. That's the constructor. Python runs it automatically the moment you create an object, and it builds the object's properties.
Now the most important trick of the whole chapter: self. When you write stack_object dot push of 3, Python secretly rewrites it. The object goes into self, and 3 goes into val.
That's why every method needs at least one parameter to receive the object. Forget self, and Python crashes with a TypeError.
Each object keeps its own data. Here two stacks live side by side and never mix.
add:
a = Stack()
b = Stack()
a.push(1)
a.push(2)
b.push(9)
print(a.pop(), b.pop())

steps.say: Your turn! Read it carefully, then pick the output.

steps.say: Want to hide a property from the outside world? Start its name with two underscores. That makes it private.
From outside the class, Python pretends it doesn't exist. You get an AttributeError.
But here's the secret: it isn't really hidden. Python just renames it. It glues an underscore and the class name in front. This is called name mangling.
So if you use the renamed version, it works perfectly from outside.
Exam trap! Mangling only happens for names written INSIDE the class. If you create a double-underscore name from outside, it keeps its name exactly.
Private methods work exactly the same way: two underscores, and they get renamed too.
Your turn!

add.why: Inside class A, __p was stored as _A__p.

steps.say: Instance variables belong to ONE object. You create them with self dot something, so every object gets its own copy.
A class variable is written directly in the class body, outside any method. There is only ONE copy, and every object shares it.
That's why every object reads the same value. Three objects were created, so counter is 3 for everyone.
add:
o1 = ExampleClass()
o2 = ExampleClass(2)
o3 = ExampleClass(4)
print(o1.counter, o3.counter, ExampleClass.counter)

steps.say: Now the biggest trap of this chapter. Writing through an object does NOT change the class variable. It creates a NEW instance variable that hides the class one, only for that object.
add:
class C:
    n = 1

a = C()
b = C()
a.n = 5
C.n = 7
print(a.n, b.n, C.n)

steps.say: __dict__ shows only an object's OWN variables. Class variables live in the class's __dict__.
add:
class C:
    n = 1

a = C()
b = C()
a.n = 5
C.n = 7

steps.say: Careful with lists. dot append changes the one shared list. No new variable is created, so everyone sees the change.
add:
class Team:
    members = []

t1 = Team()
t2 = Team()
t1.members.append('Malak')
print(t2.members)

{r:obj.x = …} → new instance variable
{g:obj.list.append(…)} → changes the shared one

steps.say: Your turn!

add.code:
class K:
    count = 0
    def __init__(self):
        K.count += 1
        self.count = 10

k1 = K()
k2 = K()
print(K.count, k1.count)

steps.say: Reading a property that doesn't exist crashes with AttributeError. In this course example, the object only gets a OR b, depending on the value.
So ask first, with hasattr. Give it the object or the class, and the name as a STRING, in quotes.
add:
class ExampleClass:
    a = 1
    def __init__(self):
        self.b = 2

obj = ExampleClass()
print(hasattr(obj, 'b'), hasattr(obj, 'a'))
print(hasattr(ExampleClass, 'b'), hasattr(ExampleClass, 'a'))

class var → visible from objects {g:✓}
instance var → NOT visible from the class {r:✗}

steps.say: Every class carries a few built-in labels. Learn these three.
Trap! Objects don't have __name__. Only classes do. To get the class name from an object, use type of the object, dot __name__.
add:
class Classy:
    pass

obj = Classy()
print(Classy.__name__, type(obj).__name__)
print(obj.__name__)

steps.say: __bases__ gives a tuple of the direct parents, in the order you wrote them. No parent written? Then the parent is object, because everything inherits from object.
add:
class A: pass
class B: pass
class C(A, B): pass
print([k.__name__ for k in C.__bases__], A.__bases__[0].__name__)

steps.say: Your turn!

add.why: x lives in the class's __dict__; y in each object's; an object's __dict__ never lists class variables.

steps.say: Inheritance: a new class, the subclass, gets everything from an existing class, the superclass. Then it can add things or change them. In diagrams, arrows go from the subclass UP to the superclass.
add: class {g:AddingStack}({b:Stack}):   ← parent goes in the brackets

steps.say: Important: Python does NOT call the parent's constructor for you. You must do it yourself, first thing in your own __init__.
Forget it, and the parent's properties are never created.
Two ways to call the parent. Through the class name, you must pass self yourself. Through super, you don't pass self.
Overriding means the subclass writes a method with the same name. Python uses the subclass version first. Here AddingStack's push also keeps a running sum.
Methods you don't override are simply inherited. Sub has no __str__ here, so Super's is used.
Your turn!
Three tools that look alike but answer three different questions. Let's take them one by one.
issubclass of A, B asks: is class A below B in the family tree? And yes, every class is a subclass of itself!
add: print(issubclass(TrackedVehicle, Vehicle), issubclass(Vehicle, TrackedVehicle), issubclass(Vehicle, Vehicle))

class Vehicle: pass
class LandVehicle(Vehicle): pass
class TrackedVehicle(LandVehicle): pass

steps.say: isinstance of an object and a class asks: was this object made from that class, or from one of its children?
add:
l = LandVehicle()
print(isinstance(l, Vehicle), isinstance(l, TrackedVehicle), isinstance(l, object))

class Vehicle: pass
class LandVehicle(Vehicle): pass
class TrackedVehicle(LandVehicle): pass

steps.say: is checks whether two names point to the very SAME object in memory. Double equals compares values instead. Here object_3 is just a second name for object_1.
add:
class SampleClass:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val

object_1 = SampleClass(0)
object_2 = SampleClass(2)
object_3 = object_1
object_3.val += 1
print(object_1 is object_2, object_3 is object_1)
print(object_1.val, object_2.val, object_3.val)

steps.say: Here's the summary to remember.
add:
{b:issubclass} → two classes
{g:isinstance} → object + class
{o:is} → same object in memory?

steps.say: Your turn!

add.code:
class A: pass
class B(A): pass

b = B()
print(isinstance(b, A), issubclass(A, B), b is B())
add.why: b is a B, so also an A; A is the parent, not the child; B() makes a brand-new object.

steps.say: When you ask for an attribute, Python searches from the bottom up: the object, its class, then the parents. It stops at the FIRST match and never looks higher.
With two parents, Python searches left to right, in the order you wrote them in the brackets.
Now the famous diamond. B and C both inherit from A, and D inherits from both. Python checks D, then B, then C, and A only at the very end, after BOTH B and C.
add: This search order is the {o:MRO}: Method Resolution Order → {b:D.__mro__}

steps.say: If you write an impossible order, like a parent BEFORE its own child, Python refuses to even create the class: TypeError.
add:
class Bottom({r:Top}, Middle) ✗  → Top is Middle's parent!
class Bottom(Middle, Top) {g:✓}

steps.say: Your turn!

add.why: MRO is D, B, C, A: B has no x, so C's x is found before A's.

steps.say: Polymorphism means: the same method call does different things depending on the object. Watch doanything. It's written only in One, but it calls self dot do_it.
add:
do_it from One
do_it from Two

steps.say: When the object is a Two, self is a Two, so Two's do_it runs. It doesn't matter where the code was written. The OBJECT decides.
Next, __str__. It decides what print of an object shows. Without it you get an ugly memory address.
Trap: __str__ must RETURN a string. Return a number and print crashes with TypeError.
add: print(obj) → calls obj.__str__() → must {r:return a str}

steps.say: Your turn! This one mixes both ideas.

add.why: Cat inherits __str__, but self.sound() runs Cat's version: polymorphism.
